label: lem:cheb0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cheb0}
For each $N \geq2$, we have 
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^Nq_j=0\quad \text{ and } \quad
 \frac1N\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j^2=\frac12.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The fact that $\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j=0$ follows because the set of zeros is symmetric about the origin.
To show the second identity, we use that
$q_j=\cos\theta_j$ and
\[
 \cos^2\theta=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2},
\]
while the equally spaced angles $2\theta_j$ in $[0,2\pi)$ make the sum of $\cos2\theta_j$ vanish.
head: environment

label: lem:cheb
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Basic identities and estimates

title: Proof
body_md:
The first identity follows immediately from \eqref{eqTX5}:
$$b_j=\sum_{k\ne j}\log|q_j-q_k|=\log N-(N-1)\log2-\log\sin\theta_j.$$
This implies that
$$\beta_j=b_j-b_* =  b_j -\max_kb_k = b_j - b_1 = \log\frac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin\theta_j}\le0.
$$ 

To deduce the identity involving the reciprocal sums, notice that,
for a polynomial $P(x)=c\prod_k(x-x_k)$ with simple zeros,
\[
 \frac{P''(x_j)}{2P'(x_j)}=\sum_{k\ne j}\frac1{x_j-x_k}.
\]
Applying this to $T_N$ and using the differential equation \eqref{eqdiff} at $q_j$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eqTX6}
 \sum_{k\ne j}\frac1{q_j-q_k} = \frac{T_N''(q_j)}{2\,T_N'(q_j)}
 =\frac{q_j}{2(1-q_j^2)}.
\end{equation}

To prove the inequality about the squared reciprocal terms,
write $T_N(x)=(x-q_j)Q_j(x)$. Then
\[
 \frac{Q_j'(q_j)}{Q_j(q_j)}=\sum_{k\ne j}\frac1{q_j-q_k},
 \qquad
 \left(\frac{Q_j'}{Q_j}\right)'(q_j)=-\sum_{k\ne j}\frac1{(q_j-q_k)^2}.
\]
Since $T_N'(q_j)=Q_j(q_j)$, $T_N''(q_j)=2Q_j'(q_j)$, and the third derivative satisfies $T_N'''(q_j)=3Q_j''(q_j)$,
\[
 \sum_{k\ne j}\frac1{(q_j-q_k)^2} = -\frac{Q_j''(q_j)}{Q_j(q_j)} + \frac{Q_j'(q_j)^2}{Q_j(q_j)^2}
 =\left(\frac{T_N''(q_j)}{2T_N'(q_j)}\right)^2-\frac{T_N'''(q_j)}{3T_N'(q_j)}.
\]
Differentiating the Chebyshev differential equation gives
\[
 (1-x^2)T_N'''(x)-3xT_N''(x)+(N^2-1)T_N'(x)=0.
\]
At $x=q_j$ and using also \eqref{eqTX6}, this yields
\[
 \frac{T_N'''(q_j)}{T_N'(q_j)}= \frac{3q_jT_N''(q_j)}{(1-q_j^2)T_N'(q_j)}-\frac{N^2-1}{1-q_j^2}
 =\frac{3q_j^2}{(1-q_j^2)^2}-\frac{N^2-1}{1-q_j^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \sum_{k\ne j}\frac1{(q_j-q_k)^2}=
 \biggl(\frac{q_j}{2(1-q_j^2)}\biggr)^2 - 
 \frac13\biggl(\frac{3q_j^2}{(1-q_j^2)^2}-\frac{N^2-1}{1-q_j^2}\biggr)=
 \frac{N^2-1}{3(1-q_j^2)}-\frac{3q_j^2}{4(1-q_j^2)^2}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 \sum_{k\ne j}\frac1{|q_j-q_k|^2}
 \lesssim\frac{N^2}{\sin^2\theta_j}.
\]

To prove that $d_N\simeq N^{-2}$, 
observe that the gaps between consecutive Chebyshev nodes are smallest at the endpoints. Hence,
\[
 \min_{j\ne k}|q_j-q_k| = |q_1-q_2|
 =\cos\frac{\pi}{2N}-\cos\frac{3\pi}{2N}
 \simeq N^{-2}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:weighted
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weighted}
For every integer $m\ge2$ and every $0\le a\le m$,
\[
 \sum_{\ell\ne j}\frac{\sin^a\theta_\ell}{|q_j-q_\ell|^m}
 \lesssim_m \frac{N^m}{\sin^{m-a}\theta_j}.
\]
The same estimate holds, up to a constant depending on $m$ and the bi-Lipschitz constant, if $q_j-q_\ell$ is replaced by $Q(q_j)-Q(q_\ell)$ for a uniformly bi-Lipschitz map $Q$ on $[-1,1]$.
head: environment
name: Weighted reciprocal sums

title: Proof
body_md:
Use
\[
 |q_j-q_\ell|=2\sin\frac{\theta_j+\theta_\ell}{2}
 \left|\sin\frac{\theta_j-\theta_\ell}{2}\right|.
\]
We shall use the symmetric estimate
\[
 \sin\frac{\theta_j+\theta_\ell}{2}
 \ge \frac12\max\{\sin\theta_j,\sin\theta_\ell\}.
\]
Indeed, for fixed $u\in(0,\pi)$, the minimum of
\(\sin((u+v)/2)\) over \(v\in[0,\pi]\) is attained in one of the end-points. Then it follows that
\[
 \sin\frac{u+v}{2}\ge \min\left\{\sin\frac u2,\sin\frac{u+\pi}2\right\}= 
 \min\left\{\sin\frac u2,\cos\frac u2\right\}\geq \sin\frac u2\,\cos\frac u2
 \ge\frac12\sin u,
\]
and the same argument with $u$ and $v$ interchanged gives the claim. 

Since $|\sin\frac x2|\gtrsim |x|$ for $x\in[-\pi,\pi]$, we also have
\[
 \left|\sin\frac{\theta_j-\theta_\ell}{2}\right|\gtrsim\frac{|j-\ell|}{N}.
\]
Thus
$$|q_j-q_\ell| \gtrsim \max\{\sin\theta_j,\sin\theta_\ell\}\,\frac{|j-\ell|}{N},$$
and so
\[
 \frac{\sin^a\theta_\ell}{|q_j-q_\ell|^m}
 \lesssim_m \frac{N^m}{\sin^{m-a}\theta_j}\frac1{|j-\ell|^m}.
\]
Now the result follows by summation.

label: eqn:sibling_dist
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x\in K_n$, and let $y\in\mathcal{Y}_\ell(x)$
for some $1\leq\ell\leq n$.

If $\ell=1$, then, writing $p=\hat{x}$, we have
\[
|x-y|
=
a_{n-1}(p)r^{n-1}
|Q_p(q_{j(x)})-Q_p(q_{j(y)})|.
\]
Thus, by the bi-Lipschitz property of $Q_p$ and
Lemma~\ref{lem:cheb},
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:sibling_dist}
cr^{n-1}\frac{\sin\theta_{j(x)}}N
\leq |x-y|
\leq 4C_1Nr^{n-1},
\end{equation}
for some absolute constant $c>0$.
This proves the desired estimates for $\ell=1$.

Suppose now that $\ell\geq2$. Set
\[
u=P^{(\ell-1)}(x),
\qquad
v=P^{(\ell-1)}(y).
\]
Then $u$ and $v$ are distinct children of their
common parent
\[
p=P^{(\ell)}(x)=P^{(\ell)}(y).
\]
Let $j=j(u)$ and $k=j(v)$, so that $j\ne k$.

We first estimate the distances from $x$ and $y$
to $u$ and $v$, respectively. By the bounds
on the scaling factors and on the polynomials
$Q_p$, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
|x-u|
&\leq
CC_1N\left(r^{n-1}+\cdots+r^{n-\ell+2}\right)
+CC_1Nr^{n-\ell+1}\sin\theta_j
\\
&\leq
CC_1Nr^{n-\ell+1}
\left(r+\sin\theta_j\right)
\leq
CC_1Nr^{n-\ell+1}\sin\theta_j,
\end{aligned}
\]
where we used that
$r=N^{-1/s}<N^{-1}\lesssim\sin\theta_j$.

The same argument, applied to $y$, gives
\[
|y-v|
\leq
CC_1Nr^{n-\ell+1}\sin\theta_k.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eqn:two-tails}
|x-u|+|y-v|
\leq
CC_1Nr^{n-\ell+1}
\max\{\sin\theta_j,\sin\theta_k\}.
\end{equation}

On the other hand, since $u$ and $v$ are
siblings, the bi-Lipschitz property of $Q_p$
and the estimate in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted} yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
|u-v|
&=
a_{n-\ell}(p)r^{n-\ell}
|Q_p(q_j)-Q_p(q_k)|
\geq
\frac12 r^{n-\ell}|q_j-q_k|
\\
&\geq
c r^{n-\ell}
\max\{\sin\theta_j,\sin\theta_k\}
\frac{|j-k|}{N}
\geq
c r^{n-\ell}
\frac{\max\{\sin\theta_j,\sin\theta_k\}}N.
\end{aligned}
\]

Combining this estimate with
\eqref{eqn:two-tails}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
|x-y|
&\geq |u-v|-|x-u|-|y-v|
\\
&\geq
r^{n-\ell}
\max\{\sin\theta_j,\sin\theta_k\}
\left(\frac cN-CC_1Nr\right)
\\
&\geq
\frac{c}{2N}r^{n-\ell}
\max\{\sin\theta_j,\sin\theta_k\}
\geq cr^{n-\ell}N^{-2},
\end{aligned}
\]
provided that $N$ is sufficiently large
so that $CC_1N^2r\leq c/2$.
This is possible because $s<1/2$ and
$r=N^{-1/s}$.

For the upper bound, using the same
decomposition and the preceding estimates,
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
|x-y|
&\leq |x-u|+|u-v|+|v-y| \leq CC_1Nr^{n-\ell}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the desired estimates on $|x-y|$.
The identity
\[
\#\mathcal{Y}_\ell(x)=(N-1)N^{\ell-1}
\]
follows directly from the tree structure.

Finally, the convergence of $K_n$ in the
Hausdorff distance and the $s$-Ahlfors
regularity of the limiting measure follow
by the standard symbolic-space argument,
using the separation and diameter bounds
established above. See, for example,
\cite[Proposition 2.1]{DJJ23}.

label: lem:Delta1-profile
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Delta1-profile}
As long as $N$ is chosen sufficiently large depending on $s$ and $M$, we have 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Delta1-profile-expansion}
\Delta_1(k)
=
C_{1,p}+\beta_k
+
\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}
\left(
LP_{m+1,p}(q_k)+A_{m,p}(q_k)
\right)
+
E_{1,M,p}(q_k),
\end{equation}
where
\[
C_{1,p}=(N-1)\log\rho_p+b_*,
\]
$A_{1,p} = 0$, and $A_{m,p}\in\mathcal P_m$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m$ for $2 \le m \le M-1$. Moreover, we have the bounds
\[
\|A_{m,p}\|_{\mathrm{coeff}}
\lesssim_M N\tau^m, \qquad |E_{1,M,p}(q_k)|\lesssim_M N\tau^M,
\qquad 1\le k\le N,
\]
and each $A_{m,p}$ is determined uniquely by $P_{2,p}, \dotsc, P_{m,p}$.
head: environment
name: Expansion of $\Delta_1$

label: eqDelta1k
title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:new-children}, the definition of $x= x_k$, we see that
\[
\Delta_1(k)
=
(N-1)\log\rho_p
+
\sum_{\ell\ne k}
\log|Q_p(q_k)-Q_p(q_\ell)|.
\]
Write
\[
Q_p(q_k)-Q_p(q_\ell)
=
(q_k-q_\ell)
\left(
1+\sum_{\nu=1}^{M-1}D_{\nu,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
\right),
\]
where
\[
D_{\nu,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
=
\frac{P_{\nu+1,p}(q_k)-P_{\nu+1,p}(q_\ell)}
     {q_k-q_\ell}.
\]
Then we have
\begin{align}\label{eqDelta1k}
\Delta_1(k)
& =
(N-1)\log\rho_p
+\sum_{\ell\ne k}\log|q_k-q_\ell| + \sum_{\ell\ne k} \log\left|
1+\sum_{\nu=1}^{M-1}D_{\nu,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
\right|\nonumber\\
& = (N-1)\log\rho_p  + b_*+ \beta_k+ \sum_{\ell\ne k} \log\left|
1+\sum_{\nu=1}^{M-1}D_{\nu,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
\right|,
\end{align}
where $\beta_k$ is as in \eqref{eqn:bj}.
We now consider the last term in \eqref{eqDelta1k}. The
polynomial $D_{\nu,p}$ has total degree at most $\nu$ in
$(q_k,q_\ell)$. Moreover, by the mean value theorem and
\eqref{eq:new-correction-bounds},
\[
|D_{\nu,p}(q_k,q_\ell)|
\le
\|P_{\nu+1,p}'\|_\infty
\lesssim_M\tau^\nu.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\left|
\sum_{\nu=1}^{M-1}D_{\nu,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
\right|
\lesssim_M\tau < 1/2
\]
if $\tau$ is sufficiently small (i.e., if $N$ is sufficiently large), so we are justified in expanding the $\log$ above.

To ease notation, write $D_\nu=D_{\nu,p}(q_k,q_\ell)$. 
Then
\begin{align}
\log  \left \lvert {1+\sum_{\nu=1}^{M-1}D_\nu }  \right \rvert   
={}&
\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}
\frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}
\left(\sum_{\nu=1}^{M-1}D_\nu\right)^j
+
O_M(\tau^M)
\nonumber\\
={}&
\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}
\frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}
\sum_{\substack{\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_j=1 \\ \nu_1 + \cdots + \nu_j < M    }}^{M-1}
D_{\nu_1}\cdots D_{\nu_j}
+
O_M(\tau^M),
\label{eq:log-D-expansion}
\end{align}
where all the terms for which $
\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j\ge M$ are included in the remainder. Grouping the remaining
terms according to $m=\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j$ for $1 \le m \le M-1$
we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-D-grouped}
\log \left \lvert {1+\sum_{\nu=1}^{M-1}D_\nu}  \right \rvert   
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}
\mathcal A_{m,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
+
O_M(\tau^M),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-Amathcal}
\mathcal A_{m,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
=
\sum_{j=1}^{m}
\frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}
\sum_{\substack{\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j=m\\
\nu_i\ge1}}
\prod_{i=1}^j
D_{\nu_i,p}(q_k,q_\ell).
\end{equation}

The term with $j=1$ in \eqref{eq:def-Amathcal} is simply
$D_{m,p}$. Hence
\begin{align}
\mathcal A_{m,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
={}&
D_{m,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
+
\sum_{j=2}^{m}
\frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}
\sum_{\substack{\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j=m\\
\nu_i\ge1}}
\prod_{i=1}^j
D_{\nu_i,p}(q_k,q_\ell).
\label{eq:Amathcal-split}
\end{align}
After summing in $\ell\ne k$, the first term gives
\[
\sum_{\ell\ne k}
D_{m,p}(q_k,q_\ell)
=
LP_{m+1,p}(q_k).
\]
We define the remaining part by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-Amp}
A_{m,p}(q_k)
:=
\sum_{\ell\ne k}
\sum_{j=2}^{m}
\frac{(-1)^{j+1}}{j}
\sum_{\substack{\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j=m\\
\nu_i\ge1}}
\prod_{i=1}^j
D_{\nu_i,p}(q_k,q_\ell).
\end{equation}
For $m=1$ the second sum is empty, and hence $
A_{1,p}=0$. Formula \eqref{eq:def-Amp} also makes clear why $A_{m,p}$ depends only
on the polynomials $
P_{2,p},\ldots,P_{m,p}$, but not on $P_{m+1, p}$. 
Indeed, when $j\ge2$ and $\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j=m$, we necessarily have
\[
1\le\nu_i\le m-1.
\]
Thus $P_{m+1,p}$ occurs only in the linear term
$LP_{m+1,p}$.

We next verify the degree and size estimates for $A_{m,p}$. Since
$D_{\nu_i,p}$ has total degree at most $\nu_i$, every product in
\eqref{eq:def-Amp} has total degree at most
\[
\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j=m
\]
in $(q_k,q_\ell)$. Expanding $A_{m,p}$ into monomials, summing in $\ell$, and using the identities
\[
\sum_{\ell\ne k}q_\ell^a
=
S_a-q_k^a,
\qquad
S_a=\sum_{\ell=1}^Nq_\ell^a,
\]
we see that $A_{m,p}$ is a polynomial in $q_k$ of degree at most
$m$. Furthermore, 
$|D_{\nu_i,p}|
\lesssim_M\tau^{\nu_i}$, and
so every product in \eqref{eq:def-Amp} is bounded by
\[
C_M\tau^{\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j}
=
C_M\tau^m.
\]
Since, for fixed $M$, there are only $O_M(1)$ possible compositions
of $m$, and the outer sum in \eqref{eq:def-Amp} contains at most $N$ terms, we obtain
\[
\|A_{m,p}\|_{\mathrm{coeff}}
\lesssim_M
N\tau^m.
\]
Since all the polynomials involved have degree bounded in terms of \(M\), their coefficient norms are controlled by their uniform norms, with constants depending only on \(M\).

Finally, the terms omitted from \eqref{eq:log-D-grouped} contain a
total power at least $\tau^M$. For each fixed pair $(k,\ell)$ their
sum is $O_M(\tau^M)$, and hence, after summing over $\ell\ne k$,
\[
|E_{1,M,p}(q_k)|
\lesssim_M
N\tau^M,
\]
which completes the proof.

label: lem:Delta2-profile

body_md:
\label{lem:Delta2-profile}
Assume that for all $p \in K_{n-1}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:field-hypothesis-profile}
|\Lambda_{n-1,d}(p)|
\le C_MN\tau^d,
\qquad 1\le d\le M.
\end{equation}
As long as $N$ is large enough, depending on $M$, $s$, and $\eta$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Delta2-profile-expansion}
\Delta_2(k)
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}B_{m,p}(q_k)
+
E_{2,M,p}(q_k),
\end{equation}
where $B_{m,p}\in\mathcal P_m$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m$, and we have the bounds 
\[
\|B_{m,p}\|_{\mathrm{coeff}}
\lesssim_M N\tau^m, \qquad |E_{2,M,p}(q_k)|\lesssim_{M, \eta} N\tau^M,
\qquad 1\le k\le N.
\]
Moreover, each polynomial $B_{m,p}$ is determined uniquely by the polynomials $P_{2,p}, \dotsc P_{m,p}$ and depends 
only. More precisely, $B_{m,p}$ depends only on the exterior field
coefficients $\Lambda_{n-1,d}(p)$ and on the correction
polynomials $P_{\nu,p}$ with $\nu\le m$.
In particular, it is independent of $P_{m+1,p}$.
head: environment
name: Expansion of $\Delta_2$

title: Proof
body_md:
Define the small parameter $h_k=\rho_pQ_p(q_k)$, and set
\[
    H_p(h)
    =
    N\sum_{\substack{y\in K_{n-1}\\y\ne p}}
    \left(
        \log|p+h-y|-\log|p-y|
    \right),
\]
so that $\Delta_2(k)=H_p(h_k)$. We first justify the Taylor expansion of $H_p$ at the point $h_k$.
By \eqref{eq:new-correction-bounds},
\[
    \|Q_p-\operatorname{Id}\|_{C^1([-1,1])}
    \lesssim_M\tau,
\]
and hence for $\tau$ small enough, 
\[
    |Q_p(q_k)|\lesssim_M1,
    \qquad
    |h_k|\lesssim_M\rho_p.
\]
Estimate \eqref{eq:relative-scale} of Lemma~\ref{lem:prev_estimates} therefore gives
\[
    \left|\frac{h_k}{p-y}\right|
    \lesssim_{M,\eta}\tau,
    \qquad
    y\in K_{n-1},\quad y\ne p.
\]
Taking $\tau$ sufficiently small, we may assume that
\[
    \left|\frac{h_k}{p-y}\right|\le\frac12
\]
uniformly in $y$ and $k$.

Thus, for every $y\ne p$,
\[
    \log\left|1+\frac{h_k}{p-y}\right|
    =
    \sum_{d=1}^{M}
    \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{d}
    \left(\frac{h_k}{p-y}\right)^d
    +
    R_M(h_k,p-y),
\]
where the remainder satisfies $|R_M(h_k,p-y)|
\lesssim_M
\left|h_k/(p-y)\right|^{M+1}$. 
After summing over $y\in K_{n-1}\setminus\{p\}$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Delta2-Taylor}
    \Delta_2(k)
    =
    \sum_{d=1}^{M}
    \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{d}
    \Lambda_{n-1,d}(p)Q_p(q_k)^d
    +
    \mathcal R_{M,p}(h_k),
\end{equation}
by the definition of $h_k$ and $\Lambda_{n-1,d}$. The Taylor remainder satisfies 
\begin{align}
    |\mathcal R_{M,p}(h_k)|
    &\lesssim_M
    N|h_k|^{M+1}
    \sum_{\substack{y\in K_{n-1}\\y\ne p}}
    \frac{1}{|p-y|^{M+1}}
    \nonumber\\
    &\lesssim_M
    N\rho_p^{M+1}
    \sum_{\substack{y\in K_{n-1}\\y\ne p}}
    \frac1{|p-y|^{M+1}} \lesssim_M
    N\tau^{M+1}
\label{eq:Hp-Taylor-remainder}
\end{align}
where the last inequality follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:prev_estimates} with $d=M+1$ and $a=0$.


By \eqref{eq:field-hypothesis-profile},
\[
|\Lambda_{n-1,d}(p)|
\lesssim_M N\tau^d.
\]



It remains to analyze the explicit terms in
\eqref{eq:Delta2-Taylor}. For each $1 \le d \le M $, write
\[
    Q_p(q_k)^d
    =
    \left(
        q_k+\sum_{\nu=1}^{M-1}P_{\nu+1,p}(q_k)
    \right)^d.
\]
Expanding the product yields a sum of terms of the form
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Qd-typical-term}
    c(d;\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_j)\,
    q_k^{d-j}
    P_{\nu_1+1,p}(q_k)\cdots
    P_{\nu_j+1,p}(q_k),
\end{equation}
where
\[
    0\le j\le d,
    \qquad
    1\le\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_j\le M-1.
\]
The case $j=0$ is understood to give simply $q_k^d$. By the assumption \eqref{eq:new-correction-bounds},
\[
    \left|
    P_{\nu_1+1,p}(q_k)\cdots
    P_{\nu_j+1,p}(q_k)
    \right|
    \lesssim_M
    \tau^{\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j}.
\]
Consequently, after multiplication by
$\Lambda_{n-1,d}(p)$, the term
\eqref{eq:Qd-typical-term} has size
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Delta2-typical-size}
    O_M\left(
        N\tau^{d+\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j}
    \right)
\end{equation}
because we assume \eqref{eq:field-hypothesis-profile}. Moreover, its degree in $q_k$ is at most
\[
    (d-j)+\sum_{i=1}^j(\nu_i+1)
    =
    d+\sum_{i=1}^j\nu_i.
\]
Thus the same quantity
\[
    m=d+\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j
\]
controls both the order in $\tau$ and the polynomial degree.

For $1\le m\le M-1$, let $B_{m,p}$ be the sum of all the terms as in \eqref{eq:Qd-typical-term}
for which $d+\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j=m$, i.e., 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:def-Bmp}
B_{m,p}(q_k)
=
\sum_{d=1}^{m}
\frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{d}\Lambda_{n-1,d}(p)
\sum_{j=0}^{d}
\sum_{\substack{
\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_j\ge1\\
d+\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j=m
}}
c(d;\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_j)\,
q_k^{d-j}
\prod_{i=1}^jP_{\nu_i+1,p}(q_k),
\end{equation}
with the usual convention when $j=0$. In particular, the term corresponding to $d = m$ in the above is 
\[
    \frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{m}
    \Lambda_{n-1,m}(p)q_k^m.
\]
The preceding degree estimate showed that $B_{m,p}\in\mathcal P_m$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m$. Also, each summand in \eqref{eq:def-Bmp} is bounded by $C_MN\tau^m$. 
Since for fixed $M$ there are only $O_M(1)$ possible choices of
$d,j,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_j$, we obtain our desired bound on $B_{m,p}$:
\[
    \|B_{m,p}\|_{\mathrm{coeff}}
    \lesssim_M N\tau^m.
\]
Moreover, by the definition of $B_{m,p}(q_k)$ as in \eqref{eq:def-Bmp}, since the sum starts at $d =1$, we see $B_{m,p}$ is a linear combination of product of polynomials $P_{\nu+1, p}$ with $\nu+1 \le m$.

Finally, all explicit terms in \eqref{eq:Delta2-Taylor} whose total
order
\[
    d+\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_j
\]
is at least $M$ contribute $O_M(N\tau^M)$, since $\tau<1$.
Combining these terms with the Taylor remainder gives
\[
    \Delta_2(k)
    =
    \sum_{m=1}^{M-1}B_{m,p}(q_k)
    +
    E_{2,M,p}(q_k),
\]
with $|E_{2,M,p}(q_k)|
\lesssim_M N\tau^M$, proving the lemma.

name: Expansion of $\Delta_3$

label: eq:cluster-barycenter-cancellation
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $y\in K_{n-1}\setminus\{p\}$ and write its children as
\[
    z_\ell
    =
    y+u_\ell,
    \qquad
    u_\ell
    =
    \rho_yQ_y(q_\ell),
    \qquad
    1\le\ell\le N.
\]
By \eqref{eq:new-correction-normalization} and
$\sum_{\ell=1}^Nq_\ell=0$, $\sum_{\ell=1}^NQ_y(q_\ell)=0$, and therefore 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cluster-barycenter-cancellation}
    \sum_{\ell=1}^Nu_\ell=0.
\end{equation}

Recall that $x = x_k$ is a child of $p$ with index $k$, so 
\[
    x_k
    =
    p+h_k,
    \qquad
    h_k
    =
    \rho_pQ_p(q_k).
\]
By \eqref{eq:new-correction-bounds},
\[
    |Q_p(q_k)|+|Q_y(q_\ell)|
    \lesssim_M1,
\]
and hence
\[
    |h_k|\lesssim_M\rho_p,
    \qquad
    |u_\ell|\lesssim_M\rho_y.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:prev_estimates} then gives (for $N$ sufficiently large)
\[
    |h_k|
    \lesssim_{M,\eta}
    \tau|p-y|,
    \qquad
    |u_\ell|
    \lesssim_{M,\eta}
    \tau|p-y|.
\]
Thus, for $\tau$ sufficiently small, $|x_k-y|
\simeq
|p-y|$ and $ \left \lvert {u_\ell}  \right \rvert   / \left \lvert {x_k-y}  \right \rvert    \le 1/2$, uniformly in all the parameters under consideration.


We may therefore expand the logarithm around $x_k-y$ up to
order $M-1$:
\begin{align*}
    &\sum_{\ell=1}^N
    \left(
        \log|x_k-y-u_\ell|
        -
        \log|x_k-y|
    \right)  =
    \sum_{\ell=1}^N
    \log\left|1-\frac{u_\ell}{x_k-y}\right|=
    -
    \sum_{a=2}^{M-1}
    \frac1a
    \frac{\sum_{\ell=1}^N u_\ell^a}
         {(x_k-y)^a}
    +\mathcal R_y,
\end{align*}
where the linear term in $u_\ell$ (corresponding to $a=1$)
vanishes by \eqref{eq:cluster-barycenter-cancellation}.
Since
\[
    \left|\frac{u_\ell}{x_k-y}\right|
    \lesssim_{M,\eta}\tau
\]
and $|x_k-y|\approx |p-y|$, the remainder satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
    |\mathcal R_y|
    &\lesssim_M
    \sum_{\ell=1}^N
    \left|\frac{u_\ell}{x_k-y}\right|^M\lesssim_{M,\eta}
    N\frac{\rho_y^M}{|p-y|^M}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently, by Lemma~\ref{lem:prev_estimates}
with $d=a=M$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \sum_{\substack{y\in K_{n-1}\\y\ne p}}
    |\mathcal R_y|
    &\lesssim_{M,\eta}
    N\sum_{\substack{y\in K_{n-1}\\y\ne p}}
    \frac{\rho_y^M}{|p-y|^M}\lesssim_{M,\eta}N\tau^M.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the total contribution of these remainders
is of the required order, uniformly in the generation.

We next expand
\[
    (x_k-y)^{-a}
    =
    (p-y+h_k)^{-a}
\]
around $p-y$. Up to terms of total order at least $M$,
this produces terms of the form
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cluster-general-term}
    c_{a,b}\,
    \frac{
        \rho_y^a\rho_p^b
    }{
        (p-y)^{a+b}
    }
    \left(
        \sum_{\ell=1}^N Q_y(q_\ell)^a
    \right)
    Q_p(q_k)^b,
\end{equation}
where
\[
    a\ge2,
    \qquad b\ge0,
\]
and $c_{a,b}$ depends only on $a$ and $b$.
The case $b=0$ is independent of $q_k$ and will be
retained as the constant part of the corresponding profile.


We now expand the polynomial perturbations in both $Q_y^a$ and
$Q_p^b$. A typical monomial in
\[
    Q_y(q_\ell)^aQ_p(q_k)^b
\]
has the form
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cluster-corrected-monomial}
    q_\ell^{a-r}
    q_k^{b-s}
    \prod_{i=1}^r
        P_{\nu_i+1,y}(q_\ell)
    \prod_{j=1}^s
        P_{\mu_j+1,p}(q_k),
\end{equation}
where
\[
    0\le r\le a,
    \qquad
    0\le s\le b, \qquad \text{ and } 1\le\nu_i,\mu_j\le M-1.
\]
Set
\[
    \sigma
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^r\nu_i
    +
    \sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j.
\]
Since \eqref{eq:new-correction-bounds} holds both at $y$ and at $p$,
the product of the polynomials in
\eqref{eq:cluster-corrected-monomial} is bounded by
\[
    C_M\tau^\sigma.
\]

We claim that the contribution obtained from
\eqref{eq:cluster-general-term} and
\eqref{eq:cluster-corrected-monomial}, after summing over
$y\in K_{n-1}\setminus\{p\}$, is bounded by
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cluster-general-bound}
    C_MN\tau^{a+b+\sigma}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the sum over the $N$ children of $y$ contributes at most a
factor $C_MN$, and hence the absolute value of the corresponding term
is bounded by
\[
    C_MN\tau^\sigma
    \sum_{\substack{y\in K_{n-1}\\y\ne p}}
    \frac{\rho_y^a\rho_p^b}
         {|p-y|^{a+b}}.
\]
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:prev_estimates} with exponent $a+b$ and with
the power of $\rho_y$ equal to $a$, we obtain
\[
    \sum_{\substack{y\in K_{n-1}\\y\ne p}}
    \frac{\rho_y^a\rho_p^b}
         {|p-y|^{a+b}}
    \lesssim_{M, \eta}
    \tau^{a+b},
\]
since $a\ge2$. This proves
\eqref{eq:cluster-general-bound}.

We now organize the expansion according to its total order. Set
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cluster-total-order}
    m
    =
    a+b+\sigma.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:cluster-general-bound}, every term of total order $m$ is
bounded by $C_MN\tau^m$. Moreover, its degree in the child variable $q_k$ is also at most $m$. Indeed, the
only factor depending on $q_k$ in
\eqref{eq:cluster-corrected-monomial} is
\[
    q_k^{b-s}
    \prod_{j=1}^sP_{\mu_j+1,p}(q_k),
\]
whose degree is at most
\[
    (b-s)
    +
    \sum_{j=1}^s(\mu_j+1)
    =
    b+\sum_{j=1}^s\mu_j
    \le
    a+b+\sigma
    =
    m.
\]
Thus all terms of total order $m$ form a polynomial in $q_k$ of
degree at most $m$.

The same bookkeeping gives the triangular dependence needed later.
Since $a\ge2$, from
\[
    m=a+b+\sigma
\]
we have terms of the form \eqref{eq:cluster-corrected-monomial} must satisfy $\nu_i, \mu_j \le \sigma \le m-2$. Consequently the terms of total order $m$ depend only on
\[
    P_{\nu+1,z},
    \qquad
    z\in K_{n-1},
    \qquad
    1\le\nu\le m-2.
\]

For $2\le m\le M-1$, let $C_{m,p}^{(3)}$ be the sum of all explicit
terms for which
\[
    a+b+\sigma=m.
\]
Then $C_{m,p}^{(3)}
\in
\mathcal P_m$ and 
\[
    \|C_{m,p}^{(3)}\|_{\mathrm{coeff}}
    \lesssim_M
    N\tau^m.
\]
The terms with $b=0$ are independent of $q_k$ and are included as the
constant terms of $C_{m,p}^{(3)}$. A nonconstant term must have $b\ge1$. Since $a\ge2$, every
nonconstant term has total order
\[
    m=a+b+\sigma\ge3.
\]
Thus $C_{2,p}^{(3)}$ is constant, and the first possible non-constant
cluster polynomial occurs with $m \ge 3$, which corresponds to $\tau^3$.

It remains to estimate the discarded terms. All explicit terms for which the total order satisfies
\[
    a+b+\sigma\ge M
\]
are bounded, after summation, by
\[
    C_MN\tau^M
\]
using \eqref{eq:cluster-general-bound} and $\tau<1$. The Taylor remainder arising from the expansion of
$(p-y+h_k)^{-a}$ is estimated using Lemma \ref{lem:prev_estimates}. Namely, every such term
contains a factor of the form
\[
\frac{\rho_y^a\rho_p^b}
{|p-y|^{a+b}}
\]
with $a+b\ge M$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:prev_estimates} gives again an
$O_M(N\tau^M)$ contribution. Collecting all discarded terms into $E_{3,M,p}$ (including the first Taylor remainder from the first expansion of the $\log$) we conclude that
\[
    |E_{3,M,p}(q_k)|
    \lesssim_M
    N\tau^M,
    \qquad
    1\le k\le N.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:Delta3-profile-expansion}.

body_md:
\label{lem:higher-basic-error}
Fix $M\ge2$, $\eta > 0$, and suppose that $K_m$ have been constructed for $0 \le m \le n$ so as to satisfy the standing assumptions \eqref{eq:old-children}-\eqref{eq:old-scale-bound} and \eqref{eq:current-scale-bound}-\eqref{eq:new-children}. Assume in addition that we have the bound
\[

\lesssim_MN\tau^d,
\qquad
1\le d\le M,
\]
uniformly for $p\in K_{n-1}$. Then for $N$ chosen large enough, depending on $M$, $s$, and $\eta$, the following holds. 

For $x = x_k = p + \rho_p Q_p(q_k) \in K_n$ and $g_{n}(x) - g_{n-1}(p) = N^{-n} \left( \Delta_1(k) + \Delta_{2}(k) + \Delta_3(k) \right)$ defined as usual, we have 
\begin{align}
\Delta_1(k)+\Delta_2(k)+\Delta_3(k)
={}&(N-1)\log\rho_p+b_*+\beta_k \nonumber\\
&+\sum_{m=1}^{M-1}
\bigl(LP_{m+1,p}(q_k)+R_{m,p}(q_k)\bigr)
+E_{M,p}(q_k),
\label{eq:combined-profile-expansion}
\end{align}
where $R_{m,p}\in\mathcal P_m$ is a polynomial of degree at most $m$, and
\[
\|R_{m,p}\|_{\mathrm{coeff}}\lesssim_MN\tau^m, \qquad |E_{M,p}(q_k)|
\lesssim_{M, \eta } N\tau^M,
\qquad 1\le k\le N.
\]
Moreover, the polynomial $R_{m,p}$ is determined uniquely by the polynomials 
\[
    P_{\nu+1,z},
    \qquad
    z\in K_{n-1},\quad 1\le \nu\le m-1.
\]
In particular, it is independent of all corrections
$P_{m+1,z}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $p$ is the $j$-th child of $q$.  Since the children of
$q$ were constructed using $Q_q$,
\[
S_{n,d}(p)
=
\rho_q^{-d}
\sum_{\ell\ne j}
\frac1{(Q_q(q_j)-Q_q(q_\ell))^d}.
\]
The scale bound gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rho-child-parent}
\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_q}
=
r\frac{a_n(p)}{a_{n-1}(q)}
\lesssim_{M,\eta}
Nr\sin\theta_j.
\end{equation}

We first consider $d\ge2$. Since $Q_q$ is bi-Lipschitz as in \eqref{eq:Q-bilip}, we apply Lemma \ref{lem:weighted} with $a = 0$ to see that 
\[
\sum_{\ell\ne j}
\frac1{|Q_q(q_j)-Q_q(q_\ell)|^d}
\lesssim_{d,M}
\frac{N^d}{\sin^d\theta_j}.
\]
Hence we conclude 
\begin{align*}
N\rho_p^d|S_{n,d}(p)|
&\lesssim_{M,\eta}
N(Nr)^d\sin^d\theta_j
\frac{N^d}{\sin^d\theta_j} = C_{M,\eta}N\tau^d.
\end{align*}

It remains to treat $d=1$, where the absolute-value estimate above
would lose a logarithm.  By \eqref{eq:Q-close-id},
\[
Q_q(q_j)-Q_q(q_\ell)
=
(q_j-q_\ell)(1+\varepsilon_{j\ell}),
\qquad
|\varepsilon_{j\ell}|\lesssim_M\tau.
\]
For $\tau$ sufficiently small,
\[
\frac1{Q_q(q_j)-Q_q(q_\ell)}
=
\frac1{q_j-q_\ell}
+
O_M\left(\frac{\tau}{|q_j-q_\ell|}\right).
\]
Using \eqref{eqTX21} and the Chebyshev gap estimate from the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted},
\[
\left|\sum_{\ell\ne j}\frac1{q_j-q_\ell}\right|
\lesssim
\frac1{\sin^2\theta_j},
\qquad
\sum_{\ell\ne j}\frac1{|q_j-q_\ell|}
\lesssim
\frac{N\log N}{\sin\theta_j}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
|S_{n,1}(p)|
\lesssim_M
\rho_q^{-1}
\left(
\frac1{\sin^2\theta_j}
+
\frac{\tau N\log N}{\sin\theta_j}
\right).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:rho-child-parent} and
$\sin\theta_j\gtrsim N^{-1}$ gives
\[
N\rho_p|S_{n,1}(p)|
\lesssim_{M,\eta}
N\tau+N\tau^2\log N.
\]
Since $s<1/2$, we have $\tau\log N\to0$ as $N\to\infty$; after
increasing $N$ if necessary, the last expression is
$O_{M,\eta}(N\tau)$.  This proves
\eqref{eq:sibling-field-new} also for $d=1$.

For the transmission term,
\[
N\rho_p^d\,N|F_{n-1,d}(q)|
=
N
\left(\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_q}\right)^d
|\Lambda_{n-1,d}(q)|.
\]
Using
\[
\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_q}
\lesssim_{M,\eta}
Nr
=
\frac{\tau}{N}
\]
and the definition of $X_{n-1,d}$,
\begin{align*}
\frac{
N\rho_p^d\,N|F_{n-1,d}(q)|
}{
N\tau^d
}
&\lesssim_{M,\eta}
N^{1-d}\tau^dX_{n-1,d}\\
&\le
C_{M,\eta}\tau X_{n-1,d},
\end{align*}
because $d\ge1$ and $0<\tau<1$.

For $z\ne q$, write its children as
\[
    y_\ell=z+u_\ell,
    \qquad
    u_\ell=\rho_zQ_z(q_\ell).
\]
By \eqref{eq:Q-barycenter},
\[
    \sum_{\ell=1}^N u_\ell=0.
\]

We first justify the expansion around $z$.  Since
$p=q+h$ with $|h|\lesssim_M\rho_q$, Lemma~\ref{lem:prev_estimates}
gives
\[
    |h|
    \lesssim_{M,\eta}
    \tau|q-z|.
\]
Thus, for $\tau$ sufficiently small,
\[
    |p-z|\simeq|q-z|.
\]
Similarly,
\[
    |u_\ell|
    \lesssim_M\rho_z
    \lesssim_{M,\eta}
    \tau|q-z|
    \lesssim_{M,\eta}
    \tau|p-z|.
\]
Hence the Taylor expansion in $u_\ell/(p-z)$ is uniform.

The linear term vanishes after summation in $\ell$, and therefore
\[
\sum_{\widehat y=z}(p-y)^{-d}
-
N(p-z)^{-d}
=
O_M\left(
\frac{N\rho_z^2}{|p-z|^{d+2}}
\right).
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
N\rho_p^d\,|E_{n,d}^{\mathrm{cl}}(p)|
&\lesssim_M
N^2\rho_p^d
\sum_{\substack{z\in K_{n-1}\\z\ne q}}
\frac{\rho_z^2}{|p-z|^{d+2}}\\
&\lesssim_{M,\eta}
N^2
\left(\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_q}\right)^d
\sum_{\substack{z\in K_{n-1}\\z\ne q}}
\frac{\rho_q^d\rho_z^2}{|q-z|^{d+2}}.
\end{align*}
Here we used $|p-z|\simeq|q-z|$ in the second line.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:prev_estimates} with exponent
\[
    D=d+2
\]
and $a=2$.  Since $D-a=d$, it gives
\[
\sum_{\substack{z\in K_{n-1}\\z\ne q}}
\frac{\rho_q^d\rho_z^2}{|q-z|^{d+2}}
\lesssim_{M,\eta}
\tau^{d+2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
N\rho_p^d\,|E_{n,d}^{\mathrm{cl}}(p)|
\lesssim_{M,\eta}
N^2
\left(\frac{\tau}{N}\right)^d
\tau^{d+2}
=
N^{2-d}\tau^{2d+2}.
\]
Since $d\ge1$ and $0<\tau<1$,
\[
    N^{2-d}\tau^{2d+2}
    \le
    N\tau^{d+2},
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:Ecl-field-new}.  Dividing by $N\tau^d$
gives \eqref{eq:Ecl-field-normalized}.

body_md:
\label{lem:higher-potential-new}
For $M\ge2$ and $n\ge1$, assume that
\eqref{eq:old-scale-bound}, \eqref{eq:Q-close-id}, and
\eqref{eq:Q-barycenter} hold for all generations up to $n$.
If $N$ is sufficiently large, then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Lambda-main-new}
|\Lambda_{m,d}(p)|
\le
C_{M,\eta}N\tau^d,
\qquad
1\le d\le M,
\end{equation}
for every $1\le m\le n$ and every $p\in K_m$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by induction on $m\le n$.  For $m=1$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:field-decomposition} gives $F_{1,d}=S_{1,d}$, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:field-local} yields
\[
    X_1\le C_{M,\eta}.
\]

Now let $2\le m\le n$.  Multiply \eqref{eq:field-recursion-new}, with
$m$ in place of $n$, by $N\rho_p^d$, divide by $N\tau^d$, and use
Lemmas~\ref{lem:field-local}, \ref{lem:field-evaluation}, and
\ref{lem:field-cluster}.  We obtain
\begin{align}
X_{m,d}
\le{}&
C_{M,\eta}
+
C_{M,\eta}\tau X_{m-1,d}
+
C_{M,\eta}
\sum_{t=1}^{M-d}
\tau^{t+1}X_{m-1,d+t}
+
C_{M,\eta}\tau^2
+
C_{M,\eta}\tau^{M+1}.
\label{eq:Xnd-recursion}
\end{align}
When $d=M$, the sum in $t$ is empty.

Since
\[
    X_{m-1,d+t}\le X_{m-1}
\]
and, for $\tau\le1/2$,
\[
\sum_{t=1}^{M-d}\tau^{t+1}
\le
\frac{\tau^2}{1-\tau}
\le
2\tau^2,
\]
we obtain, after enlarging the constant,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Xn-recursion}
    X_m
    \le
    C_{M,\eta}
    +
    C_{M,\eta}
    \bigl(\tau+2\tau^2\bigr)X_{m-1}.
\end{equation}

Since $ \tau=N^2r=N^{2-1/s}\rightarrow0$ as $N\rightarrow \infty$ whenever $s<1/2$, we may choose $N$ so large that
\[
    C_{M,\eta}\bigl(\tau+2\tau^2\bigr)
    \le\frac12.
\]
Then
\[
    X_m
    \le
    C_{M,\eta}
    +
    \frac12X_{m-1}.
\]
Together with the bound for $X_1$, iteration gives
\[
    X_m\le C_{M,\eta},
    \qquad 1\le m\le n.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
|\Lambda_{m,d}(p)|
\le
C_{M,\eta}N\tau^d,
\qquad
1\le d\le M,
\]
for every $1\le m\le n$ and every $p\in K_m$.

label: eq:finite-order-smallness
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $s \in (0,1/2)$ and $\eta >0$ small. Recall that for $N \ge 1$, we set $N r^s = 1$ and $\tau = N^2 r$. Since $s < 1/2$, notice that we may choose some fixed $M \ge 2$ large enough so that 
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:finite-order-smallness}
	C_MN\tau^M  = C_M N^{2M+1} r^M = C_M N^{1 + M (2 -1/s)} \le \eta,
\end{equation} 
for all $N$ large enough depending on $M$ and $\eta$. It suffices to choose, for example, $M > s/(1-2s)$. In what follows, we will choose $N$ large enough, depending on $s$ and $\eta$ without explicitly stating, so as to apply our previous Lemmas where needed.



At generation one, choosing $a_0(0) = 1$, we may write for $x = q_k \in K_1$,
\begin{align*}
	g_1(x) = g_1(q_k) = N^{-1} \sum_{j \ne k} \log  \left \lvert {q_k -q_j}  \right \rvert    = \frac{b_k}N = \frac{b^*}N + \frac{\beta_k}N
\end{align*}
With the constant $c_1 = b^*/N$, we see that $e_1(x) = e_1(q_k) = 0$.
                   
               
                                     
             
                                                       
Of course the first choice, $a_0(0) =1$ satisfies $1 \le a_0(0) \lesssim_\eta N$. 
	
	
We now argue by induction on the generation $n$. Namely, assume we have thus far constructed $K_{n-1}$ so that for all $1 \le m \le n-2$ and all $z \in K_m$, we have
\begin{align}\label{eqn:ind_hypothesis}
	1 \le a_{m}(z) \lesssim_\eta N \sin \theta_{j(z)}, \; \; \sum_{k=1}^N Q_z(q_k) = 0, \; \; \|Q_z - \mathrm{Id} \|_{C^1([-1,1])}  \lesssim_M \tau,
\end{align}
and so that for each $p \in K_{n-1}$
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:induction-parent-simple}
	g_{n-1}(p)
	=
	c_{n-1}
	+
	N^{-(n-1)}
	\bigl(
	\beta_{j(p)}+e_{n-1}(p)
	\bigr),
	\qquad
	|e_{n-1}(p)|\le\eta.
\end{equation}
We now aim to build $K_n$, but we need to do so in a non-circular way: the first step is to choose the $a_{n-1}(p)$ for $p \in K_{n-1}$. Just as in the construction of Section \ref{sec:basic-construction}, we define $a_{n-1}(p)$ by the equation 
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:scalar-choice-simple}
	\log a_{n-1}(p)
	=
	\frac{N}{N-1}
	\bigl(
	\eta-\beta_{j}-e_{n-1}(p)
	\bigr),
\end{equation}
where we write $j = j(p)$ for the index of $p$. Since $\beta_j\le0$ from Lemma \ref{lem:cheb} and since $ \left \lvert {e_{n-1}(p)}  \right \rvert    \le \eta$ by induction, 
we have $a_{n-1}(p)\ge1$. Moreover, using $\beta_j
=
\log\tfrac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin\theta_j}$ and $\sin\theta_1\simeq N^{-1}$, we estimate from above,
\begin{align*}
	a_{n-1}(p)
	&=
	\exp\left[
	\frac{N}{N-1}
	\bigl(
	\eta-\beta_j-e_{n-1}(p)
	\bigr)
	\right]
	\\
	&\lesssim_\eta
	\exp\left(
	-\frac{N}{N-1}\beta_j
	\right) =
	\left(
	\frac{\sin\theta_j}{\sin\theta_1}
	\right)^{N/(N-1)}
	\lesssim_\eta
	N\sin\theta_j.
\end{align*}
Thus with this choice of $a_{n-1}(p)$, we indeed have the bounds 
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:geometric-bound-simple}
	1
	\le
	a_{n-1}(p)
	\lesssim_\eta
	N\sin\theta_j,
\end{equation}
and so all of our scalars $a_{n-1}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:current-scale-bound}, the induction hypothesis for the next generation. 

Our basic estimates by induction \eqref{eqn:ind_hypothesis} show that the estimates from Section \ref{sec:higher-potential} hold. Indeed, we may apply Lemma \ref{lem:higher-potential-new} to the generation $n-1$ to see that 
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:field-at-current-generation}
	|\Lambda_{n-1,d}(p)|
	\lesssim_M
	N\tau^d,
	\qquad
	1\le d\le M,
	\qquad
	p\in K_{n-1}.
\end{equation}
Using the above bounds, we see that we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:polynomial-renormalization} to obtain the polynomials
\[
P_{2,p},\ldots,P_{M,p},
\qquad
p\in K_{n-1},
\]
satisfying \eqref{eq:new-correction-bounds} and
\eqref{eq:new-correction-normalization}, and define the new deformations $Q_{p}$  for $p \in K_{n-1}$ as in \eqref{eq:new-deformation}: 
\begin{align*}
	Q_p(t) = t + P_{2,p}(t) + \cdots + P_{M,p}(t), \; \; p \in K_{n-1}.
\end{align*}
Then $K_{n}$ is constructed from $K_{n-1}$ as always, by replacing $p \in K_{n-1}$ by its $N$ children $x_k$ as in \eqref{eq:new-children}, with $\rho_p=a_{n-1}(p)r^{n-1}$:
\begin{align*}
	x_k = p + \rho_p Q_p(q_k), \; \; 1 \le k \le N.
\end{align*}
Notice that Lemma \ref{lem:polynomial-renormalization} also gives us our desired estimates on the maps $Q_p$ for $p \in K_{n-1}$:
\begin{align*}
	\sum_{k=1}^N Q_p(q_k) = 0, \; \; \| Q_p - \mathrm{Id}  \|_{C^1([-1,1])} \lesssim_M \tau.   
\end{align*}
Having completed the construction of \(K_n\), we turn to the estimates
 estimates on $g_n (x)$. 

 Let $x = x_k \in  K_n$ have index $k$ and parent $\hat{x} = p \in K_{n-1}$. We again write $j = j(p)$ for the index of $p$. As in the argument preceding Lemma \ref{lem:basic-ind}, we write 
\begin{align*}
	g_{n}(x_k) - g_{n-1}(p) = N^{-n} \left( \Delta_1(k) + \Delta_2(k) + \Delta_3(k)  \right),
\end{align*}
and Lemma \ref{lem:polynomial-renormalization} tells us that our $Q_p$ are chosen so as to yield
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:renormalized-step-simple}
	\Delta_1(k)+\Delta_2(k)+\Delta_3(k)
	=
	(N-1)\log\rho_p+b_*+\beta_k+E_{M,p}(q_k),
\end{equation}
with error satisfying 
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:EM-simple}
	|E_{M,p}(q_k)|
	\lesssim_M
	N\tau^M.
\end{equation}
In particular, we may write using the induction hypothesis,
\begin{align*}
	g_n(x_k)
	&=
	g_{n-1}(p)
	+
	N^{-n}
	\bigl(
	\Delta_1(k)+\Delta_2(k)+\Delta_3(k)
	\bigr)
	\\
	&=
	c_{n-1}
	+
	N^{-n+1}
	\bigl(
	\beta_j+e_{n-1}(p)
	\bigr)
	\\
	&\quad
	+
	N^{-n}
	\Bigl[
	(N-1)
	\bigl(
	\log a_{n-1}(p)+(n-1)\log r
	\bigr)
	+
	b_*+\beta_k+E_{M,p}(q_k)
	\Bigr].
\end{align*}
By \eqref{eq:scalar-choice-simple}, the choice of $a_{n-1}(p)$, we have 
\[
N\bigl(
\beta_j+e_{n-1}(p)
\bigr)
+
(N-1)\log a_{n-1}(p)
=
N\eta,
\]
so we can rewrite 
\[
g_n(x_k)
=
c_n
+
N^{-n}
\bigl(
\beta_k+ e_n(x)
\bigr),
\]
where
\begin{equation}
	\label{eq:cn-recursion}
	c_n
	=
	c_{n-1}
	+
	N^{-n}
	\bigl[
	(N-1)(n-1)\log r+b_*+N\eta
	\bigr], \; \; \; e_{n}(x) = E_{M,p}(q_k) 
\end{equation}
Since $ \left \lvert {e_n(x)}  \right \rvert    =   \left \lvert {E_{M, p}(q_k)}  \right \rvert    \le C_M N \tau^M \le \eta$ for $N$ large enough, by \eqref{eq:finite-order-smallness}, this concludes the proof by induction. Moreover, by \eqref{eq:cn-recursion},
\[
|c_n-c_{n-1}|
\le C_{N,r,\eta}\,nN^{-n}.
\]
Since this bound is summable in $n$, the sequence
$(c_n)$ converges as $n\to\infty$.
